entities.name: Great white shark
entities.fact: Great white sharks can sense the faint electrical fields given off by the muscles and heartbeat of hidden prey.

entities.name: Hammerhead shark
entities.fact: A hammerhead's wide head spreads its eyes and electrical sensors across a broad span, helping it sweep the seabed for buried rays.

entities.name: Tiger shark
entities.fact: Young tiger sharks carry the dark stripes that give them their name, and the stripes fade as the shark matures.

entities.name: Bull shark
entities.fact: Bull sharks can live in fresh water and have been found far up the Mississippi and Amazon rivers.

entities.name: Whale shark
entities.fact: The whale shark is the largest fish alive, growing to over 12 metres while feeding on plankton and small fish.

entities.name: Mako shark
entities.fact: Makos are widely regarded as the fastest sharks, built for speed with a crescent-shaped tail and a torpedo-shaped body.

entities.name: Shortfin mako
entities.fact: Shortfin makos keep their bodies warmer than the surrounding water, which powers their famous bursts of speed.

entities.name: Longfin mako
entities.fact: The longfin mako has much longer pectoral fins than its shortfin cousin and is far more rarely seen.

entities.name: Nurse shark
entities.fact: Nurse sharks rest in groups on the seabed by day and suck prey out of crevices with a powerful vacuum-like gulp.

entities.name: Lemon shark
entities.fact: Lemon sharks return to the same mangrove nurseries where they were born to give birth to their own pups.

entities.name: Blacktip reef shark
entities.fact: Blacktip reef sharks patrol reef flats so shallow that their black-tipped dorsal fins often poke above the surface.

entities.name: Blacktip shark
entities.fact: Blacktip sharks leap and spin out of the water when chasing fish and migrate along the Florida coast in large numbers each year.

entities.name: Whitetip reef shark
entities.fact: Whitetip reef sharks can pump water over their gills while resting, so they spend the day lying motionless in reef caves.

entities.name: Grey reef shark
entities.fact: Grey reef sharks warn off intruders with a hunched, exaggerated swimming display before they attack.

entities.name: Caribbean reef shark
entities.fact: The Caribbean reef shark is the shark most often seen on feeding dives in the Bahamas and is rarely found outside the western Atlantic.

entities.name: Reef shark
entities.fact: Reef sharks are the sleek, mostly harmless sharks that patrol coral reefs, and their numbers are a good sign of a healthy reef.

entities.name: Basking shark
entities.fact: The basking shark is the second-largest fish and filters plankton through a gaping mouth as it cruises slowly along.

entities.name: Goblin shark
entities.fact: The goblin shark shoots its jaws forward to snatch prey, and its pink skin comes from blood vessels showing through.

entities.name: Greenland shark
entities.fact: Greenland sharks grow about a centimetre a year and may live for several centuries, longer than any other known vertebrate.

entities.name: Frilled shark
entities.fact: The eel-like frilled shark has around 300 needle-like teeth and may carry its young for over three years before giving birth.

entities.name: Megamouth shark
entities.fact: The megamouth shark was unknown to science until 1976, when one was hauled up tangled in a US Navy sea anchor off Hawaii.

entities.name: Cookiecutter shark
entities.fact: The small cookiecutter shark bites neat round plugs of flesh out of whales, tuna and even the rubber domes of submarines.

entities.name: Bluntnose sixgill shark
entities.fact: Most sharks have five gill slits, but the bluntnose sixgill keeps six, a trait of ancient shark lineages, and lives mostly below 200 metres.

entities.name: Broadnose sevengill shark
entities.fact: Broadnose sevengill sharks have seven gill slits rather than five and have been seen hunting seals in groups off South Africa.

entities.name: Sand tiger shark
entities.fact: Sand tiger embryos eat their siblings in the womb, so only one pup from each uterus survives to birth.

entities.name: Thresher shark
entities.fact: Thresher sharks whip their enormous tails, which can be as long as their bodies, to stun fish before eating them.

entities.name: Common thresher shark
entities.fact: The common thresher's scythe-like upper tail lobe can make up half of its total length.

entities.name: Bigeye thresher shark
entities.fact: The bigeye thresher has huge upward-facing eyes for hunting in dim water hundreds of metres down, where it spends its days.

entities.name: Pelagic thresher
entities.fact: Pelagic threshers rise to a reef cleaning station at Malapascua in the Philippines each dawn to have parasites picked off by cleaner wrasses.

entities.name: Blue shark
entities.fact: Blue sharks cross whole oceans, with tagged individuals travelling from New England to Spain and back.

entities.name: Oceanic whitetip shark
entities.fact: Oceanic whitetips were blamed for many of the deaths of USS Indianapolis sailors adrift in the Pacific in 1945.

entities.name: Silky shark
entities.fact: Silky sharks get their name from the smooth feel of their skin and are among the most heavily fished sharks in the world.

entities.name: Dusky shark
entities.fact: Dusky sharks grow slowly and do not breed until about 20 years old, which makes them very vulnerable to overfishing.

entities.name: Sandbar shark
entities.fact: Sandbar sharks have an unusually tall dorsal fin and were once the mainstay of the shark fishery on the US east coast.

entities.name: Spinner shark
entities.fact: Spinner sharks charge up through schools of fish and burst from the water spinning, sometimes turning three times in the air.

entities.name: Porbeagle
entities.fact: The porbeagle, a cold-water cousin of the great white, keeps its muscles warm and ranges as far north as Iceland and Norway.

entities.name: Salmon shark
entities.fact: The salmon shark can hold its body temperature well above that of the cold North Pacific, letting it chase salmon in near-freezing seas.

entities.name: Spiny dogfish
entities.fact: Spiny dogfish carry their pups for up to two years, one of the longest pregnancies of any vertebrate.

entities.name: Small-spotted catshark
entities.fact: The small-spotted catshark lays its eggs in curly-tendrilled cases known as mermaid's purses and is one of the commonest sharks around Britain.

entities.name: Nursehound
entities.fact: The nursehound is a large spotted catshark of the eastern Atlantic that lays its eggs in tough cases attached to seaweed.

entities.name: Angelshark
entities.fact: Angelsharks are flat, ray-like sharks that bury themselves in sand and lunge upward at passing fish in a split second.

entities.name: Pacific angelshark
entities.fact: The Pacific angelshark lies buried in sand off California and Mexico and snaps upward at passing fish faster than the eye can follow.

entities.name: Wobbegong
entities.fact: Wobbegongs are flattened, carpet-patterned sharks that lie in wait on reefs, with a fringe of skin flaps hiding their mouths.

entities.name: Spotted wobbegong
entities.fact: The spotted wobbegong grows to about 3 metres and lies camouflaged on Australian reefs, occasionally biting divers who step on it.

entities.name: Tasselled wobbegong
entities.fact: The tasselled wobbegong has a fringe of branching skin lobes around its head and has been photographed swallowing a bamboo shark whole.

entities.name: Ornate wobbegong
entities.fact: The ornate wobbegong is a carpet shark of eastern Australian reefs that lies camouflaged on the bottom by day and hunts at night.

entities.name: Zebra shark
entities.fact: Zebra sharks are born with dark stripes that break up into leopard-like spots as they grow, so adults are often called leopard sharks in Australia.

entities.name: Leopard shark
entities.fact: Leopard sharks gather in warm shallows off California each summer, with pregnant females basking in the waters off La Jolla.

entities.name: Epaulette shark
entities.fact: The epaulette shark can walk across exposed reef flats on its fins and survive for hours with almost no oxygen.

entities.name: Bamboo shark
entities.fact: Bamboo sharks are small, slender reef sharks that lay eggs, and their egg cases are a staple of public and home aquariums.

entities.name: Brownbanded bamboo shark
entities.fact: The brownbanded bamboo shark is born with dark bands that fade with age and can survive for hours out of water on exposed reef flats.

entities.name: Port Jackson shark
entities.fact: Port Jackson sharks lay spiral-shaped eggs that the mother wedges into rock crevices.

entities.name: Swell shark
entities.fact: The swell shark glows green under blue light and can gulp water to double its size and wedge itself into a crevice when threatened.

entities.name: Horn shark
entities.fact: The horn shark has a sharp spine in front of each dorsal fin and crushes sea urchins and molluscs with flat, molar-like back teeth.

entities.name: Lanternshark
entities.fact: Lanternsharks are small deep-sea sharks that glow along their bellies, hiding their silhouettes from predators looking up.

entities.name: Velvet belly lanternshark
entities.fact: The velvet belly lanternshark glows along its underside and even on its dorsal spines, which may warn predators off.

entities.name: Dwarf lanternshark
entities.fact: The dwarf lanternshark is probably the smallest shark in the world, fully grown at around 20 centimetres long.

entities.name: Ninja lanternshark
entities.fact: The ninja lanternshark, a black glowing shark described in 2015, was named by the describer's young cousins, and its species name honours Jaws author Peter Benchley.

entities.name: Kitefin shark
entities.fact: The kitefin shark, found down to around 1,800 metres, is the largest known glowing vertebrate at up to about 1.8 metres long.

entities.name: Portuguese dogfish
entities.fact: The Portuguese dogfish has been caught at nearly 3,700 metres, deeper than any other shark known.

entities.name: Gulper shark
entities.fact: Gulper sharks live on deep slopes and have only one or two pups every couple of years, so their populations collapse quickly under fishing.

entities.name: Leafscale gulper shark
entities.fact: The leafscale gulper shark, named for its leaf-shaped scales, lives on continental slopes down to about 2,400 metres.

entities.name: Pacific sleeper shark
entities.fact: The Pacific sleeper shark is a sluggish giant of cold northern waters that has been recorded at depths of around 2,000 metres.

entities.name: Sleeper shark
entities.fact: Sleeper sharks are sluggish cold-water sharks of the deep, and the flesh of some species is toxic until it is fermented or dried.

entities.name: Bramble shark
entities.fact: The bramble shark is covered in large thorn-like denticles and is so rarely encountered that little is known about its life.

entities.name: Prickly shark
entities.fact: The prickly shark is a bulky Pacific relative of the bramble shark, covered in thorn-like scales, and lives on deep slopes.

entities.name: Sharpnose sevengill shark
entities.fact: The sharpnose sevengill is a slender deep-water shark with seven gill slits and large green eyes.

entities.name: Crocodile shark
entities.fact: The crocodile shark, the smallest of the mackerel sharks, has huge eyes for hunting in dim water and snaps hard when hauled aboard.

entities.name: Viper dogfish
entities.fact: The viper dogfish has needle-like fangs on jaws it can thrust forward, and it glows along its belly in the deep waters off Japan.

entities.name: Spined pygmy shark
entities.fact: The spined pygmy shark is one of the smallest sharks, about 25 centimetres long, and glows from its belly far below the surface.

entities.name: Pocket shark
entities.fact: Only two pocket sharks have ever been found, and the tiny shark's pocket glands near its front fins are thought to squirt glowing fluid.

entities.name: Night shark
entities.fact: The night shark has large green eyes and lives along the edge of the continental shelf in the Atlantic, rising to feed at night.

entities.name: False catshark
entities.fact: The false catshark is a flabby deep-water shark with a long, low dorsal fin and has been found down to about 1,500 metres.

entities.name: Smalltooth sand tiger
entities.fact: The smalltooth sand tiger is a bulky deep-water shark that lives down to around 900 metres and is rarely seen alive.

entities.name: Angular roughshark
entities.fact: The angular roughshark has tall sail-like dorsal fins and a stocky, triangular body, and lives on muddy slopes down to around 700 metres.

entities.name: Birdbeak dogfish
entities.fact: The birdbeak dogfish has an extremely long, flattened snout and lives on continental slopes down to around 1,500 metres.

entities.name: Black dogfish
entities.fact: The black dogfish is a small glowing shark of the deep North Atlantic that gathers in large schools on the continental slope.

entities.name: Smooth-hound
entities.fact: Smooth-hounds are small, harmless sharks with flat crushing teeth for eating crabs, and anglers catch them along European shores.

entities.name: Tope
entities.fact: The tope, or school shark, was heavily fished for its vitamin-rich liver oil in the 1940s and can live for over 50 years.

entities.name: Scalloped hammerhead
entities.fact: Scalloped hammerheads gather in schools of hundreds around seamounts such as Cocos Island and the Galápagos.

entities.name: Great hammerhead
entities.fact: The great hammerhead, the largest hammerhead at up to about 6 metres, uses its head to pin stingrays to the seabed.

entities.name: Smooth hammerhead
entities.fact: The smooth hammerhead has no notch in the middle of its head and ranges further into cool water than other hammerheads.

entities.name: Bonnethead
entities.fact: The bonnethead is the only shark known to eat and digest seagrass, which can make up over half of its diet.

entities.name: Winghead shark
entities.fact: The winghead shark has the widest head of any hammerhead, nearly half as wide as the shark is long.

entities.name: Silvertip shark
entities.fact: Silvertip sharks, with white edges on every fin, patrol the drop-offs of Indo-Pacific reefs and are bold around divers.

entities.name: Galápagos shark
entities.fact: Despite its name, the Galápagos shark is found around oceanic islands worldwide, including Bermuda and Ascension in the Atlantic.

entities.name: Tawny nurse shark
entities.fact: The tawny nurse shark is a docile Indo-Pacific reef shark that sucks prey from crevices and rests in groups in reef caves.

entities.name: Blacknose shark
entities.fact: The small blacknose shark has a dark smudge on its snout tip and is common in the warm shallows of the western Atlantic.

entities.name: Atlantic sharpnose shark
entities.fact: The Atlantic sharpnose shark is a small, common shark of the US Atlantic and Gulf coasts, often the first shark a beach angler catches.

entities.name: Coral catshark
entities.fact: The coral catshark hides in reef crevices by day and is small enough that it is often kept in home aquariums.

entities.name: Sicklefin lemon shark
entities.fact: The sicklefin lemon shark is the Indo-Pacific cousin of the lemon shark and is a favourite of shark-feeding dives in French Polynesia.

entities.name: Blind shark
entities.fact: The blind shark is not blind at all; it got its name because it closes its eyelids when lifted out of the water.

entities.name: Manta ray
entities.fact: Manta rays filter plankton through their gills and somersault repeatedly to stay in a dense patch of food.

entities.name: Giant manta ray
entities.fact: The giant oceanic manta can span over 7 metres across and is the largest of all rays.

entities.name: Reef manta ray
entities.fact: Reef mantas visit cleaning stations on coral reefs and can be told apart by the unique spot patterns on their bellies.

entities.name: Stingray
entities.fact: A stingray's venomous barb is a modified scale on its tail, used only in self-defence when the ray is stepped on or threatened.

entities.name: Southern stingray
entities.fact: Southern stingrays gather in the shallows of Stingray City in the Cayman Islands, where they have been hand-fed by visitors for decades.

entities.name: Blue-spotted ribbontail ray
entities.fact: The bluespotted ribbontail ray's bright blue spots warn predators that its tail carries two venomous spines.

entities.name: Bluespotted maskray
entities.fact: The bluespotted maskray has a dark mask across its eyes and is often confused with the bluespotted ribbontail ray.

entities.name: Round stingray
entities.fact: Round stingrays cause most of the stingray injuries on southern California beaches, which is why bathers do the 'stingray shuffle'.

entities.name: Common stingray
entities.fact: The common stingray of the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean was described by ancient Greek and Roman writers, who feared its venomous spine.

entities.name: Cownose ray
entities.fact: Cownose rays migrate in schools of thousands along the US east coast and feed by digging clams out of the sand.

entities.name: Eagle ray
entities.fact: Eagle rays flap their pointed wings to fly through the water and sometimes leap clear of the surface.

entities.name: Spotted eagle ray
entities.fact: Spotted eagle rays can leap clear of the water and have a white-spotted back and a whip-like tail armed with venomous spines.

entities.name: Bat ray
entities.fact: Bat rays flap over the sandy bottoms of California bays, digging up clams with their wings, and can span nearly 2 metres.

entities.name: Electric ray
entities.fact: Electric rays can deliver shocks of up to about 220 volts from kidney-shaped organs on either side of their head.

entities.name: Atlantic torpedo
entities.fact: The Atlantic torpedo is the largest electric ray, up to about 1.8 metres and 90 kilograms, and delivers shocks of around 220 volts.

entities.name: Marbled electric ray
entities.fact: The marbled electric ray of the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean stuns its prey with powerful electric shocks.

entities.name: Skate
entities.fact: Skates lay their eggs in leathery cases called mermaid's purses that often wash up on beaches.

entities.name: Common skate
entities.fact: The common skate, once abundant in European seas, can grow over 2 metres long and is now critically endangered.

entities.name: Flapper skate
entities.fact: The flapper skate is the largest skate in the world, reaching about 2.5 metres long, and lays egg cases up to about 25 centimetres long.

entities.name: Thornback ray
entities.fact: The thornback ray, the most common skate around Britain, is covered in thorny spines and lays egg cases known as mermaid's purses.

entities.name: Little skate
entities.fact: The little skate is a small, common skate of the north-west Atlantic that walks along the seabed on modified pelvic fins.

entities.name: Barndoor skate
entities.fact: The barndoor skate is one of the largest skates of the north-west Atlantic, reaching 1.5 metres, and was nearly wiped out as bycatch.

entities.name: Cuckoo ray
entities.fact: The cuckoo ray has a big dark-and-yellow eye spot on each wing and lives on sandy bottoms of the north-east Atlantic.

entities.name: Sawfish
entities.fact: A sawfish's toothed snout is lined with sensors that detect prey, and it slashes sideways to stun fish.

entities.name: Smalltooth sawfish
entities.fact: The smalltooth sawfish was once found from New York to Brazil but now survives mainly in south-west Florida, where it is protected.

entities.name: Largetooth sawfish
entities.fact: The largetooth sawfish can live in fresh water and has been caught hundreds of kilometres up rivers in Australia and Central America.

entities.name: Green sawfish
entities.fact: The green sawfish is one of the largest sawfish, reported at over 7 metres long, and is now critically endangered.

entities.name: Narrow sawfish
entities.fact: The narrow sawfish, or knifetooth sawfish, has a slimmer snout than other sawfish and is the only member of its genus, Anoxypristis.

entities.name: Guitarfish
entities.fact: Guitarfish are rays shaped like a guitar, with a flattened shark-like body, and they give birth to live young.

entities.name: Bowmouth guitarfish
entities.fact: The bowmouth guitarfish, or shark ray, has ridges of spiky thorns over its eyes and back and looks like a cross between a shark and a ray.

entities.name: Devil ray
entities.fact: Devil rays leap metres into the air and belly-flop back down in spectacular group displays off Mexico.

entities.name: Giant devil ray
entities.fact: The giant devil ray of the Mediterranean can span over 5 metres and gives birth to a single pup after a pregnancy of about two years.

entities.name: Butterfly ray
entities.fact: Butterfly rays are much wider than they are long, with a very short tail, and bury themselves in sand in warm shallows.

entities.name: Ocellate river stingray
entities.fact: The ocellate river stingray lives in the Amazon and Paraná river systems and is one of the few rays found only in fresh water.

entities.name: Giant freshwater stingray
entities.fact: A giant freshwater stingray caught in the Mekong in 2022 weighed about 300 kilograms, the largest freshwater fish ever recorded.

entities.name: Short-tail stingray
entities.fact: The short-tail stingray is among the largest stingrays, reaching over 2 metres across and about 350 kilograms.

entities.name: Pelagic stingray
entities.fact: The pelagic stingray is the only stingray that lives in the open ocean rather than on the seabed.

entities.name: Yellow stingray
entities.fact: The yellow stingray is a small, speckled ray of the Caribbean that can change its colour to blend in with the sand.

entities.name: Atlantic stingray
entities.fact: The Atlantic stingray tolerates fresh water and has a permanent population in Florida's St Johns River.

entities.name: Roughtail stingray
entities.fact: The roughtail stingray is one of the largest whiptail stingrays in the Atlantic, over 2 metres across, with rows of thorns on its tail.

entities.name: Diamond stingray
entities.fact: The diamond stingray of the eastern Pacific has a diamond-shaped disc and a tail longer than its body armed with a venomous spine.

entities.name: Black-blotched stingray
entities.fact: The blotched fantail ray can grow nearly 2 metres across and is often seen at cleaning stations on Indo-Pacific reefs.

entities.name: Honeycomb stingray
entities.fact: The honeycomb stingray has a tail up to three times its body length and a net-like pattern on its back.

entities.name: Cowtail stingray
entities.fact: The cowtail stingray has a flap of skin under its tail like a feather, and its rough skin has been used to make shagreen leather.

entities.name: Porcupine ray
entities.fact: The porcupine ray has no stinging spine at all; instead its back is covered in sharp thorns.

entities.name: Blue stingray
entities.fact: The blue stingray of southern African waters has blue markings on its back and is a favourite of shore anglers.

entities.name: Pink whipray
entities.fact: The pink whipray is a large Indo-Pacific stingray that often rests in piles of several individuals on sandy lagoon floors.

entities.name: Mangrove whipray
entities.fact: The mangrove whipray spends its youth in mangroves and lagoons of the Indo-Pacific and has a white-spotted dark back.

entities.name: Sixgill stingray
entities.fact: The sixgill stingray lives in deep water and is the only stingray with six pairs of gill slits instead of five.

entities.name: Thorntail stingray
entities.fact: The thorntail stingray of Australia, New Zealand and South Africa carries rows of thorns along its tail and can reach 1.8 metres across.

entities.name: Bluntnose stingray
entities.fact: The bluntnose stingray of the western Atlantic has a rounded snout and glides over sandy flats from Massachusetts to Brazil.

entities.name: Leopard whipray
entities.fact: The leopard whipray has a leopard-like pattern of dark rings and was only separated from the honeycomb stingray as a species in 2008.

entities.name: Flounder
entities.fact: Flounders start life with an eye on each side, then one eye migrates across the head as the fish settles flat on the seabed.

entities.name: Flatfish
entities.fact: Flatfish lie on one side on the seabed, and the side facing down loses its colour while the upper side matches the sand.

entities.name: Halibut
entities.fact: Halibut are the largest flatfish, and Atlantic halibut can grow to over 2 metres long and more than 300 kilograms.

entities.name: Dover sole
entities.fact: Dover sole hide in sand by day and hunt worms and small crustaceans at night across the north-east Atlantic.

entities.name: Plaice
entities.fact: Plaice are easy to recognise by the bright orange spots scattered across their brown upper side.

entities.name: Turbot
entities.fact: Turbot are prized food fish with a nearly circular body and can change their colour to match the gravel they lie on.

entities.name: Lemon sole
entities.fact: Despite its name, the lemon sole is not a true sole but a right-eyed flounder found around the British Isles.

entities.name: Dab
entities.fact: The dab is a small, common flatfish of north European sandy seabeds, with rough skin and a lateral line that curves over the pectoral fin.

entities.name: Brill
entities.fact: Brill are close relatives of turbot with a more oval body and a frilled front edge to the dorsal fin.

entities.name: Summer flounder
entities.fact: The summer flounder, or fluke, is a left-eyed flatfish prized by anglers on the US east coast and can change colour to match the bottom.

entities.name: Atlantic halibut
entities.fact: Atlantic halibut can live for 50 years and females take about 10 years to mature, so the species is easily overfished.

entities.name: Pacific halibut
entities.fact: Pacific halibut are a mainstay of Alaskan fisheries, and anglers call the biggest ones, over 45 kilograms, barn doors.

entities.name: Peacock flounder
entities.fact: The peacock flounder is covered in bright blue rings and can change its pattern to match the reef in seconds.

entities.name: Stargazer
entities.fact: Stargazers bury themselves in sand with only their upward-facing eyes showing, and some species can give an electric shock.

entities.name: Monkfish
entities.fact: Monkfish lie flattened on the seabed and twitch a fleshy lure on their heads to draw fish into their enormous mouths.

entities.name: Megrim
entities.fact: The megrim is a slender, left-eyed flatfish of deep European slopes that was long overlooked by British diners and sold mostly to Spain.

entities.name: Winter flounder
entities.fact: Winter flounder move inshore in winter and carry antifreeze proteins in their blood to survive icy New England waters.

entities.name: Witch flounder
entities.fact: The witch flounder lives on deep muddy seabeds of the North Atlantic and is sold under names like Torbay sole and grey sole.

entities.name: Tonguefish
entities.fact: Tonguefish are tongue-shaped flatfish with both eyes on the left side, and one species lives beside hydrothermal vents in the Pacific.

entities.name: Starry flounder
entities.fact: The starry flounder can be left- or right-eyed and is named for the star-shaped spiny scales scattered across its skin.

entities.name: European flounder
entities.fact: The European flounder moves far up rivers into fresh water and returns to the sea to spawn.

entities.name: Greenland halibut
entities.fact: The Greenland halibut's migrating eye stops at the top edge of its head, so it can swim upright as well as lie flat.

entities.name: Flathead
entities.fact: Flatheads are flattened Australian fish with a wide, bony head that lie half-buried in sand waiting for prey.

entities.name: Olive flounder
entities.fact: The olive flounder, or hirame, is the most widely farmed flatfish in Japan and South Korea and is served raw as sashimi.

entities.name: Pancake batfish
entities.fact: The pancake batfish is a round, flattened fish of the Gulf of Mexico seabed that hops along on arm-like fins.

entities.name: Red-lipped batfish
entities.fact: The red-lipped batfish of the Galápagos is a poor swimmer and instead walks across the seabed on its stiff, limb-like fins.
